Abstract
This review explores the interplay of thermal and magnetic properties in phase 
change materials (PCMs), covering both conventional (organic/inorganic) and 
advanced (magnetic nanocomposite) systems for energy storage and spintronics. 
We examine the fundamental principles of PCMs, categorizing them into organic, 
inorganic, and magnetic nanocomposites, while analyzing their thermal properties 
including latent heat, thermal conductivity, and cycling stability. The review highlights 
how magnetic nanoparticle integration (e.g., Fe3O4, Co) enhances PCM performance 
through magneto-thermal coupling, for achieving faster phase transitions under 
magnetic fields and latent heat gains in Fe-doped vanadium oxides. The key 
magnetic parameters—saturation magnetization (Ms), remanence (Mr), coercivity (Hc), 
and hysteresis—demonstrating their critical role in governing PCM functionality. The 
thermal-magnetic synergy enables innovative applications including: magnetocaloric-
enhanced thermal energy storage (TES) systems with high exergy efficiency, spin 
caloritronic devices exploiting the spin Seebeck effect, and non-volatile phase-
change memory with ultrafast switching. Advanced material systems such as 
Fe-doped Ge2Sb2Te5 alloys and LaFeSi high-entropy PCMs are analyzed for their 
phase-dependent magnetic properties. Challenges in interfacial stability, hysteresis 
losses, and scalable manufacturing are discussed alongside cutting-edge solutions 
like 2D-material encapsulation and AI-driven material design. The review concludes 
with future directions emphasizing quantum-enhanced characterization, bio-inspired 
thermal management, and space-grade PCM development, positioning thermal-
magnetic PCMs as pivotal for next-generation energy and computing technologies.

2  Fundamental principles and types of phase change materials
Phase-change materials store/release energy via latent heat during phase transitions, 
governed by entropy and enthalpy changes. Magnetic PCMs integrate ferromagnetic, 
paramagnetic, or antiferromagnetic components (e.g., Fe-doped Ge-Sb-Te,F e3O4, 
CoFeB) to align magnetic ordering with phase transitions, enabling spintronics and 
energy storage applications [53–58]. Their magnetic properties (saturation magnetiza­
tion, hysteresis) arise from electron spin interactions and magnetic ordering. Strongly 
correlated electron systems (e.g., chalcogenides) exhibit magneto-thermal coupling 
via electronic-lattice interactions [59–62]. First-principles calculations reveal inter­
facial electronic modifications in PCM/spin-filter layers, influencing spin-dependent 
trans- port [63, 64]. Thermal-magnetic synergy leverages magnetic nanoparticles for 
enhanced thermal conductivity and magneto-thermal resistance, enabling high resis­
tance ratios at room temperature [65, 66]. Multifunctional hybrids (core-shell structures, 
para-/antiferromagnetic composites) optimize form stability and nucleation kinetics 
[67–70]. Applications include thermomagnetic energy harvesting (e.g., FeNi alloys) and

transfer performance.

These materials benefit from higher volumetric energy density compared to organic 
PCMs. However, they suffer from phase segregation during repeated melting- 
solidification cycles, particularly in salt hydrate systems where incongruent melting 
can lead to component separation [85]. Metallic PCMs, while exhibiting excellent 
thermal properties, face challenges with corrosion and high density [86]. Recent 
advances in microencapsulation and nanostructuring have shown promise in 
mitigating these issues while preserving their inherent thermal advantages.

3  Thermal properties of phase change materials
Phase-change materials exhibit unique thermal/magnetic properties enhanced through 
material engineering and nanoparticle integration for energy storage and spintronics 
due to their ability to store and release thermal energy through phase transitions. PCMs 
store thermal energy via latent heat during phase transitions; nanoparticle integration 
(e.g.,TiO2, graphite) enhances thermal conductivity (2–10W/mK) and heat transfer rates. 
Critical properties include thermal conductivity (k), latent heat (∆H), and stability, char­
acterized by DSC/TGA [9, 93–101]. These materials are characterized by their latent 
heat and thermal conductivity, which are crucial for efficient energy storage systems.
3.1  Latent heat
PCMs store energy during phase transitions, at a constant temperature, which is advan­
tageous for maintaining a stable thermal environment. Organic PCMs have a latent heat 
100–200 kJ/kg, inorganic 150–300 kJ/kg [2, 5, 83, 91, 102, 103].
3.2  Thermal conductivity
Enhanced via graphene (2–4 W/mK) [2], CNTs (50–200% improvement), or magnetic 
nanoparticles (Fe3O4-paraffin) [2, 104–108]. The inherent low thermal conductivity 
of PCMs like paraffin wax can be improved by incorporating materials such as multi-
walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs), which can enhance thermal conductivity by 
48%, and TiO2 nanoparticles have been used to increase thermal conductivity by 37% in 
n-nonadecane [109, 110].
3.3  Cycling stability
Shape stabilization techniques such as encapsulation and the use of porous matrices 
improve the structural integrity of PCMs, preventing leakage during phase changes 
[111]. Organic PCMs demonstrate less than 10% degradation after undergoing 1,000 
thermal cycles, indicating good but limited cyclic stability. Encapsulated inorganic 
PCMs show superior durability and maintain performance for more than 10,000 cycles. 
Nanoencapsulation technology proves to be particularly effective, preserving 95% of the 
original thermal energy storage efficiency even after extended cycling, demonstrating 
excellent retention of the phase-change properties and structural integrity of the mate­
rial over time. These metrics collectively highlight the improved thermal cycling stabil­
ity achieved through material encapsulation strategies, with nanoencapsulation showing 
the most promising results in minimizing performance degradation [112–117].
3.4  Thermal response
Innovative material designs, particularly Fe-doped carbon aerogel composites, enable 
PCMs to exhibit responsive behavior to multiple external stimuli, including light, elec­
tricity, and magnetic fields. Additionally, eutectic PCM formulations demonstrate supe­
rior thermal properties with enhanced stability across broader temperature ranges. 
Regarding energy dynamics, these systems show a significant reduction in activation 
energy when subjected to magnetic fields, though this comes with the trade-off of 
thermal-magnetic hysteresis effects (energy losses during cyclic magnetization-demag­
netization under temperature gradients), that influence the material’s phase transition

4  Magnetic properties of PCMs
PCMs are emerging for energy storage and spintronics due to their dual thermal-mag­
netic functionality. Lever- aging high latent heat capacity, PCMs enable efficient thermal 
management in batteries and electronics while exhibiting tunable magnetic properties 
for spin-based applications [138]. Magnetic nanoparticles (MNPs) like Fe3O4 enhance 
PCM thermal conductivity and enable magnetic field-responsive phase transitions, 
reducing supercooling and accelerating melting/solidification [108, 139, 140]. MNP dop­
ing improves thermal conductivity via phonon transport, enables precise magnetic tem­
perature control, and enhances nucleation rates for efficient energy storage [117, 141, 
142]. Photoelectromagnetic PCMs (e.g., Mn-doped GeTe) activated by light/magnetic 
stimuli enable precise thermal management and non-volatile spin switching in spintron­
ics [143]. PCMs integrated with magnetic tunnel junctions (MTJs) leverage the spin See­
beck effect for energy-efficient data storage [117].
PCMs also play a crucial role in electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding for elec­
tronic applications. incorporating carbonaceous materials, like multi-walled carbon 
nanotubes, enhances their EMI effectiveness while ensuring efficient energy storage 
[144]. Additionally, 3D-networked polymer composites enhance thermal conductiv­
ity and provide multifunctional thermal management and electromagnetic protection 
[145]. These advancements facilitate faster heat transfer, making these materials suitable 
for rapid thermal response applications. Overall, integrating advanced materials into 
PCMs shows promise for enhancing both EMI performance and thermal conductivity, 
paving the way for improved energy storage systems and spintronic applications. This 
magnetic functionality creates opportunities for energy conversion/storage: non-con­
tact, on-demand phase transitions for thermal energy release in batteries/electronics; 
hybrid magnetocaloric-PCM systems improving cooling efficiency/waste-heat recovery;

5  Thermal-magnetic synergy mechanisms in phase change materials
Thermal-magnetic synergy in PCMs drives transformative advances in energy and com­
puting. Skyrmion- based computing leverages thermally driven motion of nanoscale 
spin textures, enabling probabilistic architectures via unidirectional skyrmion diffu­
sion in magnetic multilayers [149, 150]. Direct thermal-to-electrical conversion exploits 
PCMs with abrupt magnetoelectric phase transitions to harvest waste heat at 10–200°C 
gradients [151, 152]. Nanoscale engineering integrates PCMs with spintronics for tun­
able magnetic properties and nonlinear optical states, while magneto-ionic approaches 
enable low-power devices via electric- field-induced ion migration [153–155]. Joule 
heating management remains critical for MRAM and PCM technologies, alongside 
spin-crossover nanomaterials with thermally/magnetically switchable states [156–158]. 
Spin caloritronics, the study of heat-driven spin currents, e.g., via the spin Seebeck effect 
enables thermal-to-spin energy conversion in PCM-spintronic hybrids, harnesses the 
spin Seebeck effect in magnetic insulators, while phase-transition modulation (e.g.,VO/
(Co/Pt) heterostructures) achieves reversible magnetic anisotropy shifts (3×105 erg/cm3) 
[159–161]. Multicaloric effects couple thermal, magnetic, and electric responses for 
multifunctional platforms.
Metallized PCM microcapsules with dopamine-functionalized MNPs exhibit tunable 
responsiveness for smart textiles and spintronic buffers, while hybrid composites like 
paraffin-AP25 wax achieve 92% solar-to-thermal efficiency with magnetic stability [102, 
162]. Carbon-based composites enhance thermal storage and transfer, with magnetic 
fields improving performance in trapezoidal prism walls [2, 117]. Theoretical frame­
works (Ginzburg-Landau equation, LLG modeling support device reliability, while prac­
tical implementations include ferromagnetic carbon aerogel-PCM composites showing 
rapid magnetic-field-induced transitions [10, 118, 163]. Multicaloric effects and spin 
caloritronics enable heat-to-spin conversion, with perovskite oxides exhibiting giant 
multiphononic effects. These advances position thermal-magnetic PCMs as transforma­
tive tools for energy harvesting and smart materials [143, 164].
Integrating thermal-magnetic properties into PCMs enhances energy storage and 
spintronics through multi- functional coupling. Magnetocaloric effects in MNP-doped 
composites achieve ∆Tadi = 3–5 K/T [4, 32, 38], while magnetic fields reduce super­
cooling in Fe-doped PCMs and tune coercivity (Hc) for controlled energy release [57, 
165, 166]. The Spin-lattice interactions via phonon-spin coupling enhance heat trans­
fer through phonon-spin coupling play a crucial role in enhancing heat transfer in 
materials [31, 167]. This coupling facilitates phonon-mediated spin transport, where 
phonons (quantized sound waves) assist in the movement of spin information. Addition­
ally, it enables magnon-phonon coupled thermal transport, which involves the interac­
tion between magnons (quanta of spin waves) and phonons, leading to efficient energy 
transfer. Moreover, this interaction allows for field-tunable thermal conductivity, mean­
ing that the thermal properties of the material can be adjusted by applying external

6  Spintronics principles and fundamental properties
Spintronics exploits electron spin and magnetic moments for device functionality, 
governed by saturation magnetization (Ms), coercivity (Hc), and remanence (Mr). Key 
advances include spin-dependent phenomena, where giant magnetoresistance (GMR) 
initiated spin-based electronics, enabling current-independent magnetic material design 
[40, 178]. Material classification covers diamagnetic, paramagnetic, and ferromagnetic

7.1  Thermal energy storage (TES)
Thermal Energy Storage is a pivotal technology for synchronizing thermal energy avail­
ability with usage needs across temporal or spatial domains, thereby optimizing energy 
efficiency. This method stores energy by altering the physical or chemical state of materi­
als, such as heating, cooling, melting, or vaporizing, and later reversing these processes 
to release stored heat. TES systems are adaptable to diverse energy infrastructures, 
including renewable sources like solar and geothermal energy, as well as industrial waste 
heat recovery applications. TES strategies are broadly divided into chemical and physi­
cal approaches. Chemical TES relies on reversible reactions, such as sorption and ther­
mochemical processes, where energy is absorbed during decomposition (charging) and 
released during recombination (discharging). While thermochemical storage boasts high 
energy density, its practical implementation remains limited due to challenges in mate­
rial stability and system complexity. Physical TES, which includes sensible and latent 
heat storage, is more widely adopted due to its operational simplicity and scalability. 
Phase change materials are pivotal in TES systems due to their high energy density and 
reversible phase transitions. Coupling thermal and magnetic properties in thermal-mag­

storage mechanisms, with binary nano-enhanced PCMs (NePCMs) achieving ∆H = 185 
J/g and k = 4.2 W/m.K [77, 83, 207]. Magnetic-PCM composites enable modular TES 
with 95% geometric conformality, though challenges like corrosion mitigation and cost 
reduction persist [208, 209].

enable on-demand heat release via magnetocaloric effects and reduce charge/discharge

7.1.1  Sensible heat storage (SHS)
Sensible Heat Storage (SHS) operates by elevating the temperature of a material, either 
solid or liquid, through heat transfer mechanisms like conduction, convection, or radia­

capacity, and the temperature difference between its initial and final states [22]. The

9.2  Comparative study of magnetic phenomena in PCM-spintronic hybrids
Two competing paradigms govern magnetic field control in phase-change-material-
spintronic hybrids: the Jiles-Atherton (JA) model and spin-lattice coupling theory. The 
JA model provides computationally efficient hysteresis modeling through domain wall 
dynamics, but fails to capture atomic-scale spin-lattice interactions critical for PCM 
behavior [278–280]. In contrast, spin-lattice coupling rigorously describes electron- 
phonon-mediated angular momentum transfer, though its computational intensity 
limits real-time applications [281, 282]. At GST/CoFeAl interfaces, the JA model under­
estimates anisotropy by 40% due to omitted spin-orbit coupling (λSOC), while spin-lat­
tice theory accurately predicts anisotropy shifts but lacks hysteresis quantification [58, 
283]. For Mn-GeTe PCMs, JA’s static pinning coefficient cannot model the 25% coer­
civity reduction during thermal cycling observed experimentally, whereas spin-lattice 
MD simulations successfully capture vacancy-mediated magnon-phonon coupling (Γmp 
∝ T 3/2) [284, 285]. Both frameworks struggle with GHz-scale switching dynamics and 
multi-phase domains exhibiting 300% spin-orbit coupling variations [17, 74]. The mag­
netocaloric effect (MCE) and spin Seebeck effect (SSE) offer distinct thermal-magnetic 
conversion pathways. MCE materials like MnFe achieve high energy densities (5–15 J/
cm3) but suffer hysteresis, while NdSmNiMnO6 provides reversible operation (1–5 J/
cm3) with broader thermal ranges [286, 287].
Recent systems reach 10–15% Carnot efficiency, though narrow operating windows 
(TC ± 10 K) persist [288, 289]. YIG/Pt is a composite structure of Yttrium Iron Garnet 
(YIG) and Platinum (Pt). YIG (Y3Fe5O12) is a ferrimagnetic material with low magnetic 
loss, high-frequency stability and magneto-optical properties, used in microwave and 
optical devices, and Pt is a corrosion-resistant, dense, and ductile metal. The combi­
nation is studied in spintronics due to the interaction of their magnetic and electrical 
properties, enabling phenomena like the spin Seebeck effect and magnetoresistance. 
SSE systems generate 1 µV/K in YIG/Pt (0.1–0.5.1.5% efficiency) and 0.1–1.1 mW/cm2 
in Fe3O4, but face interfacial scattering limits [290–292]. Hybrid approaches combining 
second-order MCE materials with spintronics achieve 50−100 mW/cm3, while enhanced

spin-lattice calculations [293–295].

rics are critical for advancing PCM-spintronic devices [296–299].Transient Electronic–
Magnetic–Thermal (TEMT) frameworks enable co-optimization, with MCE excelling in 
cooling and SSE in microelectronics. It is a spintronic phenomenon where a heat gradi­

converted into a transverse voltage in an adjacent metal layer, effectively transforming

11  Opportunities, challenges and future directions
Thermal-magnetic synergy in phase change materials (PCMs) drives transformative 
advances across multiple domains. Skyrmion-based computing leverages thermally-
driven magnetic spin textures to enable probabilistic computing architectures, offering 
new paradigms for neuromorphic systems [149, 150]. Concurrently, PCMs exhibiting 
abrupt magnetoelectric transitions facilitate efficient thermal-to-electrical energy con­
version, creating novel pathways for waste heat recovery applications [151, 152]. At the 
nanoscale, integration of PCMs with spintronic elements enables dynamically tunable 
magnetic properties through controlled phase transitions, while emerging magneto-
ionic approaches exploit ion migration mechanisms to develop ultra-low power mem­
ory and logic devices [153, 155]. In spin caloritronics, the spin Seebeck effect in PCMs 
enhances thermal energy harvesting capabilities by converting thermal gradients into 
spin currents, with phase-transition modulation further enabling reversible magnetic 
anisotropy shifts for adaptive spintronic components [159–161]. Emerging frontiers 
present additional opportunities including AI-optimized PCM composites for advanced 
thermal management in space systems and smart grids, bio-inspired designs mimicking 
biological thermoregulation mechanisms, quantum-enhanced PCMs exploiting quan­
tum coherence effects, and sustainable bio-based hybrid materials utilizing eco-friendly 
constituents [34, 330, 331].
Key technical challenges in thermal-magnetic phase change materials include main­
taining the structural stability of magnetic nanoparticle (MNP)-PCM composites under 
cyclic thermal-mechanical loading and accurately quantifying spin-phonon coupling 
efficiency in functional device geometries [168, 332]. The scalable manufacturing of 
hybrid thermal-spin devices faces significant hurdles. These challenges primarily stem 
from cyclic degradation mechanisms and interfacial defects at PCM-substrate bound­
aries. Furthermore, these issues are compounded by detrimental Joule heating effects 
in magnetoresistive RAM (MRAM) systems that integrate PCM elements [28, 156, 157, 
333]. Material-level limitations involve nanoparticle agglomeration during processing; 
fundamental coercivity-remanence trade-offs in permanent magnet alloys like Nd-Fe-B, 
thermal degradation of PCMs above 600 °C, and crystalline structure-dependent varia­
tions in latent heat capacity [93, 334–337]. Persistent technical barriers encompass inter­
facial degradation kinetics, hysteresis losses during phase transitions, limited cyclability, 
manufacturing scalability constraints, nanoscale thermal resistance at interfaces, and 
high-temperature magnetic instability in operational devices [4, 338, 339]. Additional 
adoption challenges involve unresolved material stability issues, high production costs 
of specialized composites, and reliability concerns under extreme operating conditions 
[340, 341].
Critical research priorities should focus on AI-driven design of novel phase change 
materials (PCMs) accelerated by machine learning algorithms, coupled with 2D-material 
encapsulation strategies to enhance interfacial stability and thermal management [274, 
340, 342]. Development of multifunctional magnetothermal PCMs exhibiting strong 
thermal-magnetic coupling will enable next-generation devices, alongside sustainable 
composite materials utilizing eco-friendly constituents. Quantum-enhanced character­
ization techniques will pro- vide unprecedented insights into spin-thermal interactions

12  Conclusion

ing thermal-magnetic PCMs as key enablers for next-generation technologies. As these 
solutions mature from laboratory demonstrations to commercial applications, they will 
complement (rather than replace) conventional PCMs, magnetic variants serving field-
responsive applications, while carbon-enhanced and encapsulated systems dominate in 
passive thermal management. Strategic investments in scalable fabrication technologies 
will accelerate this transition, ultimately creating a diversified PCM technology portfolio 
addressing the full spectrum of energy and computing challenges.

Abstract: This review explores the interplay of thermal and magnetic properties in phase change materials (PCMs), covering both conventional (organic/inorganic) and advanced (magnetic nanocomposite) systems for energy storage and spintronics. We examine the fundamental principles of PCMs, categorizing them into organic, inorganic, and magnetic nanocomposites, while analyzing their thermal properties including latent heat, thermal conductivity, and cycling stability. The review highlights how magnetic nanoparticle integration (e.g., Fe3O4, Co) enhances PCM performance through magneto-thermal coupling, for achieving faster phase transitions under magnetic fields and latent heat gains in Fe-doped vanadium oxides. The key magnetic parameters—saturation magnetization (Ms), remanence (Mr), coercivity (Hc), and hysteresis—demonstrating their critical role in governing PCM functionality. The thermal-magnetic synergy enables innovative applications including: magnetocaloric- enhanced thermal energy storage (TES) systems with high exergy efficiency, spin caloritronic devices exploiting the spin Seebeck effect, and non-volatile phase- change memory with ultrafast switching. Advanced material systems such as Fe-doped Ge2Sb2Te5 alloys and LaFeSi high-entropy PCMs are analyzed for their phase-dependent magnetic properties. Challenges in interfacial stability, hysteresis losses, and scalable manufacturing are discussed alongside cutting-edge solutions like 2D-material encapsulation and AI-driven material design. The review concludes with future directions emphasizing quantum-enhanced characterization, bio-inspired thermal management, and space-grade PCM development, positioning thermal- magnetic PCMs as pivotal for next-generation energy and computing technologies.
